options: A single Kafka server process, holding a subset of the cluster's partitions
A separate database that stores a copy of every topic
A load balancer sitting in front of the actual Kafka servers
A client library used only by producers, never by consumers
questions.explain: A broker is one server; no single broker holds every partition of every topic, since that would defeat the purpose of partitioning.

options: The set of brokers working together, coordinated so clients see one logical system
A single broker running multiple copies of itself
A collection of unrelated, independently managed Kafka installations
A synonym for a single topic
questions.explain: A client connects to any broker in the cluster and gets routed to the broker actually leading the partition it needs.

questions.q: Why does adding more brokers help with more than just throughput?
options: It enables replication, so a partition survives its leading broker going down without data loss
More brokers always slow the cluster down and should be avoided
Extra brokers are used only for storing logs, never for serving requests
Broker count has no relationship to fault tolerance at all
questions.explain: Each partition is replicated across multiple brokers; if the leader fails, a broker already holding a replica takes over.

questions.q: What happens when the broker currently leading a partition fails?
options: A different broker that already holds a replica of that partition's data takes over as the new leader
The entire cluster shuts down immediately
All data in that partition is permanently lost
The partition is automatically merged into a different topic
questions.explain: Replication exists specifically so a replica broker can take over as leader with no data loss and only a brief interruption.
